title: iPad Game Development Is Real
summary: Learn the iPad game-development workflow in hyperPad: choose one mechanic, build with Scenes and visual Behaviors, playtest on-device, share, and...
body_markdown:
You can design, build, and test a complete 2D game directly on iPad with hyperPad. It is a visual game engine for iPad: you arrange Objects in Scenes and connect Behaviors for input, movement, collisions, scoring, UI, and game state.


Start with one mechanic and test it on the same device. When the Project is ready for other players, paid hyperPad can Publish it to the Hub or Export an Xcode project. Final App Store signing and submission normally use a Mac with Xcode.


## What you need to make a game on iPad


You need four things for a first project:


- A game engine for scenes, logic, physics, and testing
- An art app or licensed game assets
- An audio app or licensed sound effects
- A small idea you can finish


Your first game can be one screen. A platformer with one jump, a rhythm game with one short song, or a tap game with a score counter is enough to learn the full process.


## Choose an iPad game engine


The right tool depends on whether you want to write code and where you want to build.


### hyperPad


hyperPad is a 2D game engine made for iPad. You create logic in the Behavior Editor by connecting events and actions. You can place Objects in a Scene, add physics, import your own Graphics and audio, and test your game on the same iPad.


Use[hyperPad Starter](https://www.hyperpad.com/app/starter) for one free project. The paid hyperPad app removes the one-project limit and lets you Export an Xcode project for App Store publishing.


### Swift Playground


[Swift Playground](https://developer.apple.com/swift-playground/) runs on iPad and Mac. It teaches Swift and lets you build apps with SwiftUI. Apple also supports submitting finished apps to App Store Connect. Choose it when learning and writing Swift is part of your goal.


### Codea


[Codea](https://codea.io/) lets you write Lua on iPad. It suits creators who want to program their own systems and experiment with code.


### Other game engines on iPad


[Unity](https://unity.com/) can create games for iPad, but its current Editor requirements list desktop operating systems rather than iPadOS.[Xogot](https://xogot.com/) brings a Godot-based editor to Apple devices.[GDevelop](https://gdevelop.io/) offers visual, event-based game creation on several platforms, including an iPad app. Check each current product page before choosing a workflow because platform support and plan limits can change.


These engines fit different workflows. Unity is built around a traditional desktop development pipeline. Xogot brings Godot's 2D, 3D, and scripting tools to Apple devices. GDevelop combines no-code tools with 2D and 3D game creation.


hyperPad is built first for iPad, with a touch-first workflow for designing and testing 2D games with visual Behaviors. The paid hyperPad app is also compatible with Apple silicon Macs running macOS 11 or later, including MacBooks with an M1 chip or newer.


## How to make a game on iPad


### 1. Pick one mechanic


Write one sentence that describes what your player does. For example: “Tap to keep a character in the air and pass through gaps.”


That sentence gives you a useful first scope. Menus, extra levels, and polished art can wait until the mechanic feels good.


### 2. Create your first Scene


Open hyperPad and create a landscape or portrait project. Add the Objects your mechanic needs to your[first Scene](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/scenes) . A simple platformer might start with a player, a floor, and one platform.


Use basic shapes while you test. You can replace them with finished Graphics later.


### 3. Add game logic with Behaviors


[Behaviors](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/behavior-interface-overview) control what happens in your game. Connect an event to an action in the Behavior Editor.


For a basic jump:


1. Add[Started Touching](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/started-touching) to a button.
2. Connect it to[Apply Force](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/apply-force) on the player.
3. Set an upward force.
4. Press Play and adjust the value.
5. Add a state check if the player should only jump while touching the ground.


You can use the same pattern for scoring, enemy movement, health, timers, and Scene changes.


### 4. Add art and sound


Draw your own Graphics in an iPad art app or use assets with a license that fits your project. Import each file into the Asset Library and assign it to the matching Object.


If you need prototype art, start with these[free 2D game asset sources](https://www.hyperpad.com/blog/8-best-sites-for-free-2d-game-assets-templates-perfect-for-ipad-game-devs) . Check each license before you publish or sell your game.


Keep audio simple at first. One sound for a jump, hit, or score can make the mechanic easier to understand during testing.


### 5. Test on your iPad


Press play after each meaningful change. Check the game with touch controls, then hand it to someone who has not seen the project.


Watch where they pause or miss the goal. Change one issue and test again. This is more useful than adding another feature before the main mechanic works.


### 6. Publish a test version to the Hub


Publish your Project to the[hyperPad Hub](https://www.hyperpad.com/hub) when you want feedback. Ask one focused question, such as “Does the jump feel too heavy?” Specific questions lead to clearer answers.


Open Source Projects can also be Branched. Studying another creator’s Behavior Tree can help you understand how a working mechanic is organized.


### 7. Export for the App Store


When your game is ready for a wider audience, use paid hyperPad to Export it as an Xcode project. Complete the final signing and App Store submission steps on a Mac with Xcode.


Use paid hyperPad when you are ready to work across multiple Projects and export an Xcode project for an App Store release.


## Game design apps for iPad


A small set of apps can cover the rest of your workflow:


- **Graphics:** Procreate, Pixquare, or Affinity Designer
- **Music and sound:** GarageBand or Cubasis
- **Planning:** Notes, Freeform, or a paper sketch beside your iPad
- **Game building:** hyperPad for visual Behaviors, Scenes, testing, Hub publishing, and Export


Choose one tool for each job. Switching between several art or planning apps can slow down a first project.


## What kind of game should you make first?


Pick a game with one clear input and one clear goal.


**Tap game:** Tap an Object to score before the timer ends.


**One-screen platformer:** Reach a door without touching an obstacle.


**Puzzle:** Move Objects into the correct order. To practice card state, comparisons, input locking, and reset logic, use the[memory matching game blueprint](https://www.hyperpad.com/blog/how-to-make-a-memory-matching-game-on-ipad-without-coding) .


**Rhythm prototype:** Tap one lane in time with a short original track. If this interests you, follow the[FNF-style rhythm game guide](https://www.hyperpad.com/blog/how-to-make-an-fnf-style-game-on-mobile-ipad-no-code) .


A finished small game gives you something you can test, share, and improve.


## Common questions about iPad game development


### Can you develop a game entirely on iPad?


You can design, build, test, and Publish a hyperPad Project on iPad. App Store submission requires the exported Xcode project and a Mac with Xcode.


### Can you make an iPad game without coding?


Yes. hyperPad uses visual Behaviors. You connect events and actions to describe your game’s logic instead of typing traditional code.


### Is hyperPad Starter free?


Yes. hyperPad Starter lets you make one Project. Paid hyperPad removes the one-project limit and adds Xcode Export for App Store publishing.


### Can you make 3D games with hyperPad?


hyperPad is a 2D game engine. Choose it for platformers, puzzle games, rhythm games, interactive stories, simulations, and other 2D projects.


### Do you need a new iPad?


Project needs vary. Start on the iPad you have and keep your first Scene small. More complex Projects with many Objects, effects, or large assets need more device resources.


Start with one Scene and one mechanic. Test it today. You can add finished art, more levels, and App Store plans after the first version works.


Keep the first version focused on one mechanic. Test the input, result, and restart flow before adding another Scene or system.
